questions.question: List the five functions of packaging with an example product for which each is most important, and name the three levels of packaging.
questions.expected_answer: Protection from knocks, crushing, moisture, light, air and tampering (eggs in a moulded pulp tray); containment of loose or liquid product (10 kg of maize meal in a sack); information such as name, contents, mass, date, barcode and warnings (medicine carton); convenience in carrying, opening, pouring and resealing (milk bottle with a cap); promotion to attract and persuade on the shelf (printed chips bag or premium phone box). Levels: primary packaging touches the product (bottle, bag, tray); secondary groups primary packages (carton round a bottle, shrink-wrap round cans); tertiary moves goods in bulk (corrugated case, pallet and wrap).

questions.question: Explain what is meant by 'the product determines the design', listing the questions a designer asks about the product and showing how the answers decide the shape for two different products.
questions.expected_answer: The designer starts from the product, not the box, and asks: how fragile and in which direction; how heavy; liquid, powder, solid or many pieces; does it spoil; is it dangerous or must children be kept out; how will it be stored and displayed; how will it be used. For eggs: fragile to point loads and knocks, so each sits in a cup that supports its strong ends and keeps it apart from its neighbours in a stiff tray. For cough syrup: a liquid that spoils in light and is dangerous to children, with legally required information, so a narrow-necked brown bottle with a child-resistant, tamper-evident cap inside a rectangular printed carton that stacks.

questions.question: Describe how a packaging material is chosen, compare paperboard with plastic film, and justify a material choice for a single cupcake.
questions.expected_answer: Material properties (strength, stiffness, weight, moisture and grease resistance, barrier to air and light, transparency, printability, formability, cost and end of life) are matched to the product's needs in order of importance, using the least material, preferring a single recyclable material over laminates. Paperboard is stiff, light, cheap, prints and folds well and is widely recycled but softens when wet and gives no air barrier; plastic film is flexible, waterproof, sealable and cheap with good barrier when metallised but gives no stiffness and is rarely recycled. A cupcake is soft and crushable, eaten within a day and sold on appearance, so it needs stiffness and display but no barrier: a paperboard box with a card insert to hold the base and a clear film window to show the product, recyclable apart from the window, meets the needs with least material.
